title: Asia is rearming fast – but counting the wrong kind of military power
gist: Asian defence budgets are surging (Asia-Oceania military spending hit US$681bn in 2025, the fastest rise since 2009) but the author argues governments are still counting fleets and platforms rather than 'regenerative capacity' — the ability to replace lost drones/munitions, repair damaged assets and restore networks — which is what actually determines how long a war can be sustained, illustrated through contrasting bottlenecks in Japan, China and India.

themes.theme: Regenerative capacity as the real metric of military power

insights.claim: Ukraine has shown that while weapons stockpiles determine how a war begins, 'regenerative capacity' — how fast lost drones and munitions are replaced, damaged aircraft and ships repaired, and broken communications restored — determines how long a war can actually be fought.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: A durable framework for evaluating defence-sector investment: prioritise firms in replenishment, repair, maintenance, electronics and automation over pure platform manufacturers, since this is where sustained-conflict value increasingly accrues.
insights.quote: Stockpiles determine how wars begin; regenerative capacity determines how long they can be fought.
insights.locator: Ukraine has exposed what that count misses

insights.claim: Once drones, radios and software require constant replenishment, the factories, repair shops and component suppliers behind them effectively become part of the fighting system, turning defence procurement into a capital-allocation problem that current defence ministries are not structured to solve, since they are built to sign multiyear contracts for a few expensive platforms rather than fund idle factory lines, spare-parts stockpiles and repair networks in peacetime.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Identifies a structural mismatch between how defence budgets are allocated (big platform contracts) and what actually sustains wartime capability (idle-capacity funding) — a gap likely to persist and create investment opportunities for firms offering surge-capacity/maintenance contracting models.
insights.quote: Budgets buy more weapons without necessarily buying recovery.
insights.locator: That turns defence into a capital-allocation problem

insights.claim: The money in defence is shifting from delivering large platforms toward replenishing, upgrading and repairing them, a shift that channels capital to electronics, communications, automation and maintenance firms beyond the household-name weapons makers.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Directly actionable investment thesis: look beyond prime defence contractors to electronics, comms, automation and MRO (maintenance/repair/overhaul) firms as the beneficiaries of Asia's rearmament spending shift.
insights.locator: The money in defence is moving the same way

insights.claim: Military spending in Asia and Oceania reached US$681 billion in 2025, according to SIPRI, the fastest annual rise since 2009, with Japan's outlays growing 9.7% and India's 8.9%.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Confirms a broad-based Asian defence-spending upcycle (fastest since 2009), a macro tailwind for regional defence-industrial and adjacent supply-chain equities.

themes.theme: Japan's bottleneck: commercial scale, not capability

insights.claim: Nissan's Oppama plant, which built 18 million cars including the world's first mass-market EV (the Leaf) over six decades, is due to close in 2028; US defence tech firm Anduril is in talks to take over the site next to the Yokosuka naval base and retrain its workers to build military drones.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: A concrete, trackable deal (Anduril-Oppama) that would signal a real shift of civilian manufacturing capacity into Western defence-drone production in Japan — worth monitoring for confirmation and for Anduril's broader Asia-Pacific manufacturing footprint.
insights.locator: For six decades Nissan's Oppama plant

insights.claim: Japan has precision manufacturing and skilled workers but its defence business is constrained by high costs and being run as a low-margin sideline of conglomerates; Japan's arms imports rose 76% between 2021-25, with 95% of that sourced from the United States.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Quantifies Japan's near-total dependence on US arms imports (95% of a 76% import surge) even as it seeks domestic production capacity — a data point relevant to US defence exporters' Japan exposure and to Japan's push for indigenous defence-industrial scale.
insights.locator: Oppama shows Japan's version of the problem

insights.claim: China's output of civilian drones grew 37.3% last year while its arms imports fell 72%, causing it to drop out of the top 10 arms recipients for the first time since the early 1990s — reflecting a manufacturing base of thousands of drone and component makers with product cycles measured in months, built for rapid, cheap drone production.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: China's drone-manufacturing base gives it a structural mass-production advantage for regenerative capacity, but the author stresses factory output does not equal proven military power — a caveat against overweighting China's raw manufacturing scale in threat assessments.

insights.claim: Whether Chinese forces could keep communications running under jamming, coordinate across services, and match hardware with training has never been tested in combat and cannot be verified from outside — meaning China's manufacturing scale advantage does not by itself confirm battlefield-ready regenerative capacity.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: A key uncertainty for any China military-power assessment: manufacturing capacity is observable and verifiable, but combat-integration capability is not — a caution against conflating the two in geopolitical risk models.
insights.locator: But factory output does not equal military power

insights.claim: India, still the world's second-largest arms importer, has cut Russia's share of its purchases from 70% a decade ago to 40% today, diversifying to French, Israeli and other suppliers — increasing strategic autonomy but shifting the integration burden (making French jets, Russian missiles and Israeli sensors work together) inside the Indian armed forces.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Quantifies India's arms-supplier diversification trend (Russia share 70%→40%) — relevant for tracking Indian defence procurement flows toward Western/Israeli suppliers and away from Russia, and the resulting interoperability risk.
insights.locator: India shows a third type of bottleneck

insights.claim: In the May 2025 air battle between India and Pakistan, at least one Indian Rafale was shot down — a loss a French commander acknowledged while crediting Pakistan's battle handling rather than its Chinese-made jets; subsequent reporting described Pakistani fighters receiving targeting data via data link from a surveillance aircraft and firing from a range Indian pilots did not expect.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that networked targeting/data-link integration (Pakistan's approach) beat platform quality alone (India's Rafale) in a real air battle — a strong real-world data point for the thesis that integration, not just hardware, decides combat outcomes.
insights.quote: However advanced, a plane that cannot share information is an island.
insights.locator: In last May's air battle with Pakistan

insights.claim: No published figures compare how fast China, Japan and India could replace losses, repair damage or restore networks, so this new 'regenerative capacity' yardstick cannot and should not be used to rank the three militaries against each other — each has a distinct gap: China lacks a combat-tested conversion mechanism, Japan lacks commercially sustainable production scale, and India lacks affordable multi-vendor integration.
insights.speaker: David Tingxuan Zhang
insights.so_what: A clear, differentiated framework for assessing each major Asian military's specific vulnerability, useful for scenario planning around a potential Taiwan Strait, South China Sea, or India-Pakistan contingency.
insights.locator: No published figures compare how fast China, Japan and India
